title: Engineering Economics
summary: The six compound interest factors are the whole computational content, and every problem reduces to identifying which one applies. The most examined conceptual point is that MARR is an INPUT set by the organisation while IRR is an OUTPUT computed from the project — confusing them is the commonest error in the subject. Two further traps repay attention: mutually exclusive alternatives must be compared by INCREMENTAL analysis rather than by ranking their individual IRRs, and alternatives with unequal lives must be compared over a common period or by equivalent annual cost.

sections.heading: Time value of money and the interest factors
sections.body:
**The principle.** A rupee today is worth more than a rupee next year, because it can be **invested and earn interest**. Every comparison of cash flows occurring at different times must therefore convert them to a **common point in time** before they can be added or compared.

> **Cash flows at different times cannot be added directly.** They must first be brought to the same date.

**Simple and compound interest:**

| Type | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Simple interest** | **I = P n i**; total **F = P(1 + ni)** |
| **Compound interest** | **F = P(1 + i)ⁿ** |

Simple interest is used only for short periods and some statutory calculations; **all engineering economy uses compound interest**.

**The six standard factors** — every problem is one of these, and identifying which is the skill:

| Find | Given | Factor | Formula |
|---|---|---|---|
| **F** | **P** | **(F/P, i, n)** — single payment **compound amount** | **(1 + i)ⁿ** |
| **P** | **F** | **(P/F, i, n)** — single payment **present worth** | **1/(1 + i)ⁿ** |
| **F** | **A** | **(F/A, i, n)** — uniform series **compound amount** | **[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]/i** |
| **A** | **F** | **(A/F, i, n)** — **SINKING FUND** factor | **i/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]** |
| **P** | **A** | **(P/A, i, n)** — uniform series **present worth** | **[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]/[i(1+i)ⁿ]** |
| **A** | **P** | **(A/P, i, n)** — **CAPITAL RECOVERY** factor | **i(1+i)ⁿ/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]** |

**Two of the six have names worth knowing:**

| Factor | Name | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| **(A/F)** | **Sinking fund factor** | *How much must I set aside each year to accumulate a given sum?* |
| **(A/P)** | **Capital recovery factor** | *What annual amount is equivalent to a given present investment?* |

**And a useful relation between them:**

> **(A/P, i, n) = (A/F, i, n) + i**

which says that recovering capital means **replacing it (the sinking fund) plus paying interest on it** — a statement of the two things a capital charge must cover.

**Gradient series** for cash flows increasing by a constant amount **G** each period:

> **A = A₁ + G (A/G, i, n)**,  with **(A/G, i, n) = 1/i − n/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]**

and for a **geometric** gradient (increasing by a constant **percentage g**), the present worth uses a modified factor.

**Nominal and effective interest rates** — a standard source of error:

> **Effective annual rate i_eff = (1 + r/m)^m − 1**

where **r** is the **nominal annual rate** and **m** the number of **compounding periods per year**.

**A worked case:** 12% nominal compounded **monthly** gives **i_eff = (1 + 0.12/12)¹² − 1 = 12.68%**, not 12%. Compounded **continuously**, **i_eff = e^r − 1 = 12.75%**.

**So a quoted rate is meaningless without its compounding frequency**, and comparing two loans on their nominal rates alone is an error — which is why consumer credit regulation generally requires the **effective** rate to be disclosed.

**Inflation.** The relation between nominal (money) and real (constant purchasing power) rates:

> **(1 + i_nominal) = (1 + i_real)(1 + f)**

where **f** is the inflation rate. Approximately **i_nominal ≈ i_real + f** for small rates.

**The consistency rule is the point:**

> **NOMINAL (money) cash flows must be discounted at the NOMINAL rate.**
> **REAL (constant price) cash flows must be discounted at the REAL rate.**

**Mixing them systematically distorts the appraisal** — usually by discounting constant-price cash flows at a nominal rate, which penalises long-lived projects severely and is a genuine cause of under-investment in infrastructure. Both approaches give the same answer when applied consistently; either applied inconsistently does not.

sections.heading: Comparing alternatives
sections.body:
**MARR — the Minimum Attractive Rate of Return:**

> The **LOWEST rate of return the organisation is willing to accept** on an investment — a **hurdle rate**.

It is built up from:

| Component | Contribution |
|---|---|
| **Cost of capital** | What the organisation pays for funds — the weighted average cost of debt and equity |
| **Risk premium** | Higher for uncertain projects |
| **Opportunity cost** | The return available on the next-best alternative |
| Capital rationing | Raised when funds are scarce relative to opportunities |

**MARR must exceed the cost of capital**, because investing at exactly the cost of capital creates no value and leaves no margin for the forecast being wrong.

**The distinction from IRR — the most examined point in the subchapter:**

| | **IRR** | **MARR** |
|---|---|---|
| Source | **COMPUTED** from the project's cash flow | **CHOSEN** by the organisation |
| Nature | An **OUTPUT** | An **INPUT** |
| Varies with | The **project** | The **organisation**, and the risk class |
| Role | The **result to be judged** | The **standard to judge it against** |

**IRR is the rate at which NPV becomes zero.** MARR is not — and offering "the rate at which NPV becomes zero" as a definition of MARR is the standard distractor.

**The decision criteria — all equivalent for a single project:**

> **NPV at the MARR ≥ 0** → accept
> **IRR ≥ MARR** → accept
> **B/C ratio ≥ 1** → accept

**The methods of comparison:**

| Method | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Present worth (NPV)** | All cash flows discounted to the present |
| **Future worth** | All compounded to a future date |
| **Annual worth / EUAC** | All converted to an **equivalent uniform annual** amount |
| **Rate of return (IRR)** | The rate at which NPV = 0 |
| **Benefit–cost ratio** | PV of benefits ÷ PV of costs |
| Payback period | Time to recover the investment |

**Payback period is the one to be careful with**: it is simple and widely used, but it **ignores everything after the payback point** and **ignores the time value of money** (unless a discounted payback is used). A project recovering its cost in three years and then earning nothing scores better than one recovering it in four and earning for twenty. It is a **liquidity** measure, not a profitability one, and should never be the sole criterion.

**Comparing MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE alternatives — where the real errors occur:**

> **NPV ranks correctly on its own. IRR does NOT.**

**Why IRR misranks.** A **small** project with a **spectacular** rate of return can leave most of the available capital idle. Consider two alternatives with a MARR of 10%:

| Alternative | Investment | IRR | NPV at 10% |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Rs 10,000 | **40%** | Rs 5,000 |
| **B** | Rs 100,000 | **20%** | Rs 25,000 |

**A has the higher IRR but B creates five times the value.** Choosing A on its IRR leaves Rs 90,000 uninvested (or invested at the MARR, earning nothing extra). So ranking by IRR gives the wrong answer.

**The correct method is INCREMENTAL ANALYSIS:**

1. Arrange the alternatives in **increasing order of investment**.
2. Take the **lowest-cost acceptable** alternative as the current **defender**.
3. Compute the **IRR of the INCREMENT (Δ)** to the next alternative.
4. If **ΔIRR ≥ MARR**, the **larger** alternative becomes the defender; otherwise the smaller is retained.
5. Repeat through the list.

In the example, the increment B − A costs Rs 90,000 and yields the extra return; if **ΔIRR ≥ 10%** — which it is — **B is chosen**, agreeing with the NPV ranking as it must.

**Unequal lives** — the second common error:

> Alternatives with **different lives** cannot be compared by NPV over their own lives.

Two valid approaches:

| Method | How |
|---|---|
| **Least Common Multiple (LCM) of lives** | Assume **repeated replacement** until both reach a common horizon; compare NPV over that period |
| **Equivalent Uniform Annual Cost (EUAC)** | Convert each to an **annual** figure — which is **automatically comparable** regardless of life |

**EUAC is usually the more convenient**, and it is the natural method whenever lives differ, because an annual cost carries no implicit assumption about the horizon. The LCM method is used where the repetition assumption is genuinely realistic.

**Do-nothing** must always be included as an alternative where it is feasible, and it is the baseline against which the others are judged.

**Public projects — the economic appraisal:**

| Feature | Difference from a private appraisal |
|---|---|
| **Discount rate** | The **social discount rate**, generally lower than a private MARR |
| **Prices** | **SHADOW prices**, correcting for market distortions (taxes, subsidies, exchange controls, surplus labour) |
| **Externalities** | **INCLUDED** — time savings, accident reduction, environmental damage, health effects |
| Criterion | **B/C ratio ≥ 1**, or **EIRR** against the social discount rate |
| Distribution | Who gains and who loses may matter as much as the total |

**The inclusion of externalities is why a road can be economically justified while being financially unprofitable** — the toll revenue may not cover the cost, but the **time savings, reduced vehicle operating costs and improved access** may greatly exceed it. That divergence between the **financial** and the **economic** appraisal is the central concept in public project evaluation, and it is why public infrastructure is publicly funded.

**Sensitivity analysis** is not optional for any project with significant uncertainty. It tests how the conclusion changes when key inputs vary — **capital cost overrun, delay, demand shortfall, tariff, and the discount rate itself**. An appraisal presenting a single NPV or IRR without testing it has not been completed, and for a long-lived infrastructure project the **discount rate** is usually the input to which the answer is most sensitive.

sections.heading: Depreciation, replacement and valuation
sections.body:
**Depreciation** is the systematic allocation of an asset's cost over its useful life. It is an **accounting and costing** device, not a cash flow — no money changes hands — but it determines the **hire or ownership rate** charged for plant, and hence the rate analysis for every item of work that plant performs.

**The methods:**

| Method | Annual charge | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| **Straight line** | **D = (C − S)/n** | **Uniform** |
| **Sinking fund** | **D = (C − S) × i/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]** | Uniform, but **credits interest** on the accumulating fund |
| **Declining balance** | A **fixed % of the reducing BOOK value** | **Accelerated** — heavy early, light later |
| **Sum-of-years-digits** | (remaining life / Σ digits) × (C − S) | Accelerated |
| **Production (service) units** | (C − S) × (units this year / total units) | Follows **USE** |

where **C** is the initial cost, **S** the salvage value and **n** the useful life.

**Straight line** gives **book value = C − m(C − S)/n** after m years, falling **linearly** from C to S.

**The sinking fund method** recognises that money set aside **earns interest**, so the annual deposit needed is **less** than a simple division:

> For **C − S = Rs 100,000** over **10 years at 8%**: straight line sets aside Rs 10,000 a year, while the sinking fund needs only **100,000 × 0.069 = Rs 6,900**. The **accumulated interest supplies the difference** — which is precisely the point of the method.

**Declining balance never reaches zero**, since a percentage of a positive number stays positive — mathematically inconvenient but physically realistic, since most equipment retains some value. Where a specific salvage value must be reached, the rate is set as **k = 1 − (S/C)^{1/n}**.

**Which method to use** depends on how the asset actually loses value: **straight line** where deterioration is uniform, **declining balance** where the asset loses most value early (vehicles, computers), and **production units** where wear follows use rather than time (a crusher, a mixer).

**Replacement analysis** — when to replace an existing asset:

| Reason for replacement | Character |
|---|---|
| **Deterioration** | Rising maintenance and operating cost, falling reliability |
| **Obsolescence** | A better alternative exists, though the asset still functions |
| **Inadequacy** | Demand has outgrown the capacity |
| Regulatory | Emission or safety standards |

**The method:** compare the **EUAC of KEEPING** the existing asset (the **defender**) against the **EUAC of the NEW** asset (the **challenger**), and replace when the defender's EUAC exceeds the challenger's minimum.

**The defender's EUAC RISES with time**, because maintenance grows and the remaining salvage value falls. The challenger's EUAC has a **minimum** at its economic life. **The economic life is where the total EUAC is minimised** — the balance between falling capital recovery cost (spread over more years) and rising operating cost.

**The sunk cost principle** is the most important idea in replacement analysis and the most often violated:

> **The ORIGINAL COST of the existing asset is IRRELEVANT.** Only its **current market value** (what it could be sold for now) and its **future** costs matter.

A machine bought for Rs 1,000,000 five years ago and now worth Rs 200,000 should be evaluated as a Rs 200,000 asset — because that is what keeping it actually costs (the sale forgone). Refusing to replace it "because we paid a million for it" is the **sunk cost fallacy**, and it is a genuinely common and expensive error in practice.

**Break-even analysis:**

> **Break-even point: total revenue = total cost**
> **Q_BE = Fixed cost / (Selling price per unit − Variable cost per unit)**

The denominator is the **contribution per unit**. **Margin of safety** is the excess of actual output over the break-even output, expressed as a percentage — a measure of how much demand can fall before losses begin.

In a **choice between two methods** (say hand labour against a machine), the break-even is the **quantity at which their total costs are equal** — below it the low-fixed-cost method is cheaper, above it the high-fixed-cost method. That is why mechanisation pays only above a certain volume, and it is the correct framing for equipment selection decisions.

**VALUATION — determining the present worth of an existing property.**

**The methods:**

| Method | Basis | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Rental (capitalised value)** | **Net income × Year's purchase** | Income-producing property |
| **Cost (depreciation) method** | **Replacement cost less depreciation**, plus land | Owner-occupied buildings; insurance |
| **Comparative (market)** | Recent sales of **similar** property | An active market |
| **Development method** | Value after development, less the cost to develop | Land ripe for development |
| **Profit-based** | Capitalised trading profit | Hotels, cinemas, business premises |

**The rental method's arithmetic:**

> **Net income = gross rent − outgoings**
> **Year's purchase (YP) = 100 / rate of interest** = 1/i
> **Capitalised value = net income × YP**

**The year's purchase** is literally the **number of years' income a buyer will pay** for the property, and it comes from the present value of a perpetuity, **1/i**.

**Outgoings to deduct:** **repairs (about 1/12 or 8⅓% of gross rent)**, municipal and other **taxes**, **insurance**, **management and collection**, a **sinking fund** for eventual rebuilding, and an allowance for **voids** (vacancy).

**The sinking fund entry is the one candidates omit**, and it matters: since the building has a **finite life**, part of the income must be set aside to **replace** it, and only what remains is true return on capital. Omitting it overstates the value.

**The inverse relation is the substance of the concept:**

| Expected return | YP | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **5%** | **20** | **Higher** |
| 8% | 12.5 | — |
| **10%** | **10** | **Lower** |

> **A HIGHER required return gives a LOWER valuation for the same income.**

That is not an accounting artefact but an economic truth: an investor demanding more return will pay less for a given income stream. The **rate chosen therefore reflects the RISK** of that income — a secure, well-let building is capitalised at a low rate and valued highly; an uncertain one at a high rate and valued low. **Choosing the rate is the valuer's central judgement**, and it moves the answer more than any other input.

For a **limited-term** interest rather than a perpetuity, **YP = [1 − (1+i)^{−n}]/i** — the ordinary present worth of an annuity — sometimes computed at a **dual rate**, allowing separately for the remunerative rate and the sinking fund rate.

**The valuation terms**, routinely confused and examined as a set:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Book value** | Cost **less accumulated depreciation** — an **accounting** figure, unrelated to any market |
| **Salvage value** | Worth at the end of its life, sold **INTACT and working** |
| **Scrap value** | Worth of the **DISMANTLED MATERIALS** — about **10% of cost** for a building, **net of demolition** |
| **Market value** | What a willing buyer would actually pay **today** |
| **Replacement value** | The cost of an **equivalent NEW** asset at current rates |
| **Sentimental / distress value** | Above or below market, for non-economic reasons |
| **Assessed / rateable value** | For taxation |

**The salvage/scrap distinction** is whether the asset survives **as a working thing** or **only as material**. **Scrap value can be NEGATIVE**, where demolition, disposal and site restoration cost more than the materials fetch — common for reinforced concrete, and easy to overlook.

**Book value and market value can diverge sharply**: a fully depreciated machine with a book value of zero may command a substantial price, and a building whose book value is high may be unsaleable. So an engineer asked for "the value" of an asset must first establish **WHICH value is wanted**, and for what purpose — insurance, sale, taxation, compensation and accounting each require a different one.

**And throughout: LAND DOES NOT DEPRECIATE.** It is valued separately and added, which is why the worth of an old property in a good location is often almost entirely its land.

formulas.label: The six compound interest factors
formulas.note: (A/F) is the SINKING FUND factor, (A/P) the CAPITAL RECOVERY factor. Note (A/P) = (A/F) + i.

formulas.label: Effective interest rate
formulas.note: 12% nominal compounded monthly is 12.68% effective. A quoted rate is meaningless without its frequency.

formulas.label: Nominal and real rates
formulas.note: Nominal cash flows need the nominal rate; constant-price cash flows the real rate. Mixing them distorts the result.

formulas.label: MARR and IRR
formulas.expression: MARR is an INPUT chosen by the organisation. IRR is an OUTPUT computed from the project (the rate at which NPV = 0).
formulas.note: Accept when IRR ≥ MARR, or equivalently NPV at the MARR ≥ 0.

formulas.label: Comparing mutually exclusive alternatives
formulas.expression: Use INCREMENTAL analysis: order by increasing investment, and accept each increment whose ΔIRR ≥ MARR.
formulas.note: Ranking by individual IRR misranks, because a small high-IRR project leaves capital idle. NPV ranks correctly.

formulas.label: Unequal lives
formulas.expression: Compare over the LCM of lives, or by EQUIVALENT UNIFORM ANNUAL COST (EUAC)
formulas.note: EUAC is usually more convenient, carrying no implicit assumption about the horizon.

formulas.label: Depreciation methods
formulas.expression: straight line D = (C−S)/n ;   sinking fund D = (C−S)·i/[(1+i)ⁿ−1] ;   declining balance k = 1 − (S/C)^{1/n}
formulas.note: The sinking fund charge is less than straight line, because the accumulating fund earns interest.

formulas.label: Replacement analysis
formulas.expression: Compare EUAC of the DEFENDER (rising with age) against the minimum EUAC of the CHALLENGER
formulas.note: The ORIGINAL cost of the existing asset is a SUNK COST and is irrelevant — only its market value and future costs matter.

formulas.label: Break-even quantity
formulas.expression: Q_BE = Fixed cost / (Price − Variable cost per unit)
formulas.note: The denominator is the contribution per unit. Mechanisation pays only above the break-even volume.

formulas.label: Capitalised value
formulas.expression: Capitalised value = net annual income × YP,  where YP = 100/i (perpetuity) or [1 − (1+i)^{−n}]/i (term)
formulas.note: A HIGHER required return gives a LOWER valuation. Deduct a SINKING FUND from the income for eventual rebuilding.
